'''Robert Hues''' (1553 – 24 May 1632) was an English [[mathematician]] and [[geographer]]. He attended [[St Mary Hall, Oxford|St. Mary Hall]] at [[Oxford University|Oxford]], and graduated in 1578. Hues became interested in [[geography]] and [[mathematics]], and studied [[navigation]] at a school set up by [[Walter Raleigh]]. During a trip to [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]], he made observations which caused him to doubt the accepted published values for [[magnetic declination|variations of the compass]]. Between 1586 and 1588, Hues travelled with [[Thomas Cavendish]] on a [[circumnavigation]] of the globe, performing [[astronomical]] observations and taking the latitudes of places they visited. Beginning in August 1591, Hues and Cavendish again set out on another [[circumnavigation]] of the globe. During the voyage, Hues made astronomical observations in the South Atlantic, and continued his observations of the variation of the compass at various [[latitudes]] and at the [[Equator]]. Cavendish died on the journey in 1592, and Hues returned to England the following year.

In 1594, Hues published his discoveries in the [[Latin]] work ''Tractatus de globis et eorum usu'' (''Treatise on Globes and Their Use'') which was written to explain the use of the terrestrial and celestial globes that had been made and published by [[Emery Molyneux]] in late 1592 or early 1593, and to encourage English sailors to use practical astronomical navigation. Hues's work subsequently went into at least 12 other printings in Dutch, English, French and Latin.

Hues continued to have dealings with Raleigh in the 1590s, and later became a servant of [[Thomas Grey, 15th Baron Grey de Wilton]]. While Grey was imprisoned in the [[Tower of London]] for participating in the [[Bye Plot]], Hues stayed with him. Following Grey's death in 1614, Hues attended upon [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland|Henry Percy, the 9th Earl of Northumberland]], when he was confined in the Tower; one source states that Hues, [[Thomas Harriot]] and [[Walter Warner]] were Northumberland's constant companions and known as his "Three [[Magi]]", although this is disputed. Hues tutored Northumberland's son [[Algernon Percy, 10th Earl of Northumberland|Algernon Percy]] (who was to become the 10th [[Earl of Northumberland]]) at Oxford, and subsequently (in 1622–1623) Algernon's younger brother Henry. In later years, Hues lived in [[Oxford]] where he was a fellow of the university, and discussed mathematics and related subjects with like-minded friends. He died on 24 May 1632 in the city and was buried in [[Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford|Christ Church Cathedral]].

==Early years and education==
[[File:Henry Percy-9th Earl of Northumberland.jpg|thumb|left|[[Anthony van Dyck|Van Dyck]]'s portrait of [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland|Henry Percy, the 9th Earl of Northumberland]], with whom Hues was associated]]

Robert Hues was born in 1553 at [[Little Hereford]] in Herefordshire, England. In 1571, at the age of 18 years, he entered [[Brasenose College, Oxford]].<ref name=ODNB>{{cite ODNB|author=Susan M. Maxwell|contribution=Hues, Robert (1553–1632)|title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography|edition=Online|location=Oxford|date=January 2008|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/14045|last2=Harrison|first2=B.|title-link=Dictionary of National Biography}}</ref><ref>{{citation|editor=Charles Buller Heberden|editor-link=Charles Buller Heberden|title=Brasenose College Register, 1509–1909 [Oxford Historical Series; no. 55]|location=Oxford|publisher=[[Blackwell Publishing|Blackwell]] for the Oxford Historical Society|year=1909|oclc=222963720}}</ref> English [[antiquarian]] [[Anthony à Wood]] wrote that when Hues arrived at Oxford he was "only a poor scholar or servitor&nbsp;... he continued for some time a very sober and serious servant&nbsp;... but being sensible of the loss of time which he sustained there by constant attendance, he transferred himself to [[St Mary Hall, Oxford|St Mary's Hall]]".<ref>{{citation|author=Anthony à Wood|author-link=Anthony à Wood|author2=Philip Bliss|author-link2=Philip Bliss (academic)|title=Athenae Oxonienses, an Exact History of All the Writers and Bishops who have had their Education in the University of Oxford; to which are Added the Fasti; or, Annals of the said University|volume=2|edition=New|location=New York, N.Y.|publisher=Johnson Reprint Corp.|year=1967|page=534|oclc=430234}}. At Oxford, a [[servitor]] was an undergraduate student who worked as a servant for [[Oxford fellow|fellows]] of the University in exchange for free accommodation and some meals, and exemption from paying fees for lectures.</ref> Hues graduated with a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree on 12 July 1578,<ref>{{citation|author=University of Oxford|author-link=University of Oxford|editor=Joseph Foster|editor-link=Joseph Foster (genealogist)|title=Alumni Oxonienses: The Members of the University of Oxford, 1500–1714 ... Being the Matriculation Register of the University, Alphabetically Arranged, Revised and Annotated |location=Nendeln, Liechtenstein |publisher=Kraus Reprint |year=1968 |orig-year=1891 |oclc=5574505 }}, vols. 1–2. Hues is listed under the name "Hughes".</ref> having shown marked skill in [[Greek language|Greek]]. He later gave advice to the dramatist and poet [[George Chapman]] for his 1616 English translation of [[Homer]],<ref>{{citation|author=Homer|author-link=Homer|author2=George Chapman|author-link2=George Chapman|title=The Whole Works of Homer; Prince of Poetts, in his Iliads, and Odysses. Translated according to the Greeke, by Geo. Chapman|location=London|publisher=[By Richard Field and William Jaggard] for Nathaniel Butter|year=c. 1616|oclc=216610936}}</ref> and Chapman referred to him as his "learned and valuable friend".<ref>{{citation|author=Thomas Warton|author-link=Thomas Warton|title=The History of English Poetry, from the Close of the Eleventh to the Commencement of the Eighteenth Century|volume=3|location=London|publisher=Reeves and Turner|year=1871|page=442|oclc=8048047}}: see Markham, "Introduction", ''Tratatus de globis'', p. xxxv. According to another source, Chapman called Hues "another right learned, honest, and entirely loved friend of mine": see {{citation|author=Henry Stevens|author-link=Henry Stevens (bibliographer)|title=Thomas Hariot, the Mathematician, the Philosopher and the Scholar|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5171|location=London|publisher=[Privately printed at the Chiswick Press] (reproduced on Freeonlinebooks.org)|year=1900|oclc=82784574|access-date=19 April 2012}}. See also {{citation|author=Jessica Wolfe|chapter=Homer in a nutshell: George Chapman and the mechanics of perspicuity [ch. 5]|title=Humanism, Machinery, and Renaissance Literature|location=Cambridge|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=2004|pages=161–202|isbn=978-0-521-83187-1}}</ref> According to the ''[[Dictionary of National Biography|Oxford Dictionary of National Biography]]'', there is unsubstantiated evidence that after completing his degree Hues was held in the [[Tower of London]], though no reason is given for this, then went abroad after his release.<ref name=ODNB/> It is possible he travelled to [[Continental Europe]].<ref name="Markham xxxv">Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xxxv.</ref>

Hues was a friend of the [[geographer]] [[Richard Hakluyt]], who was then regent master of [[Christ Church, Oxford|Christ Church]]. In the 1580s, Hakluyt introduced him to [[Walter Raleigh]] and [[exploration|explorers]] and [[navigator]]s whom Raleigh knew. In addition, it is likely that Hues came to know [[astronomer]] and mathematician [[Thomas Harriot]] and Walter Warner at [[Thomas Allen (mathematician)|Thomas Allen]]'s lectures in mathematics. The four men were later associated with [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland|Henry Percy, the 9th Earl of Northumberland]],<ref name=ODNB/><ref>According to Kargon, "[i]t was probably through Percy (although the reverse is possible)" that Harriot came to know Hues: {{citation|author=Robert Hugh Kargon|chapter=Thomas Hariot and the Atomic View of Nature|title=Atomism in England from Hariot to Newton|location=Oxford|publisher=[[Oxford University Press|Clarendon Press]]|year=1966|pages=18–30 at 19|oclc=531838}}</ref> who was known as the "Wizard Earl" for his interest in scientific and [[alchemy|alchemical]] experiments and his library.<ref>{{citation|author=David Singmaster |title=BSHM Gazetteer: Petworth, West Sussex |url=http://www.dcs.warwick.ac.uk/bshm/zingaz/P.html#petw |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/5h1wetK8g?url=http://www.dcs.warwick.ac.uk/bshm/zingaz/P.html |archive-date=25 May 2009 |publisher=[[British Society for the History of Mathematics]] |date=28 February 2003 |access-date=7 February 2008 |url-status=dead }}. See also {{citation|author=David Singmaster |title=BSHM Gazetteer: Thomas Harriot |url=http://www.dcs.warwick.ac.uk/bshm/zingaz/LondonPeopleH.html#harriot |archive-url=https://www.webcitation.org/5h1wkdGOq?url=http://www.dcs.warwick.ac.uk/bshm/zingaz/LondonPeopleH.html |archive-date=25 May 2009 |publisher=[[British Society for the History of Mathematics]] |date=28 February 2003 |access-date=7 February 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:Thomas Cavendish.jpg|thumb|upright|An engraving of [[Thomas Cavendish]] by Willem and Magdalena van de Passe from Holland's ''[[Herōologia Anglica]]'' (''Praise of English Heroes'', 1620),<ref>{{citation|author=Henry Holland|author-link=Henry Holland (printer)|title=Herōologia Anglica, hoc est clarissimorvm et doctissimorvm aliqovt [sic: aliqvot] Anglorvm qvi florvervnt ab anno Cristi M.D. vsq' ad presentem annvm M.D.C.XX viuae effigies vitae et elogia [List of English Heroes, that is, Lifelike Images of the Lives and Epitaphs of the most Famous and Educated of the English who Flourished from the Year of Christ 1500 until the Present Year 1620]|location=[Arnhem]|publisher=Impensis C. Passaei calcographus [sic] et Iansonij bibliopolae Arnhemiensis [Printed by Jan Jansson at the expense of Crispijn van de Passe and Jan Jansson]|year=1620|oclc=6672789}}</ref> titled "Thomas Candish, [[Armiger]]. ''Animum fortuna sequatur'' [The soul follows chance]". Hues [[circumnavigation|circumnavigated]] the globe with Cavendish between 1586 and 1588.]]

Hues became interested in [[geography]] and mathematics – an undated source indicates that he disputed accepted values of [[magnetic declination|variations of the compass]] after making observations off the [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]] coast. He either went there on a fishing trip, or may have joined a 1585 voyage to [[Virginia]] arranged by Raleigh and led by [[Richard Grenville]], which passed Newfoundland on the return journey to England. Hues perhaps become acquainted with the sailor [[Thomas Cavendish]] at this time, as both of them were taught by Harriot at Raleigh's school of navigation. An anonymous 17th-century manuscript states that Hues [[circumnavigation|circumnavigated]] the world with Cavendish [[Thomas Cavendish's circumnavigation|between 1586 and 1588]] "purposely for taking the true [[Latitude]]<!--Capitalization in the source.--> of places";<ref>[[Manuscript|MS]] Rawl. B 158, [[Bodleian Library]], [[University of Oxford|Oxford]].</ref> he may have been the "NH" who wrote a brief account of the voyage that was published by Hakluyt in his 1589 work ''The Principall Navigations, Voiages, and Discoveries of the English Nation''.<ref>{{citation|author=Richard Hakluyt|author-link=Richard Hakluyt|title=The Principall Navigations, Voiages, and Discoveries of the English Nation: Made by Sea or Over Land to the Most Remote and Farthest Distant Quarters of the Earth at Any Time within the Compasse of These 1500 Years: Divided into Three Several Parts According to the Positions of the Regions Whereunto They Were Directed; the First Containing the Personall Travels of the English unto Indæa, Syria, Arabia&nbsp;... the Second, Comprehending the Worthy Discoveries of the English Towards the North and Northeast by Sea, as of Lapland&nbsp;... the Third and Last, Including the English Valiant Attempts in Searching Almost all the Corners of the Vaste and New World of America&nbsp;... Whereunto is Added the Last Most Renowned English Navigation Round About the Whole Globe of the Earth|location=London|publisher=Imprinted by George Bishop and Ralph Newberie, deputies to Christopher Barker, printer to the Queen's Most Excellent Majestie|year=1589|oclc=77435498}}</ref> In the year that book appeared, Hues was with [[Edward Wright (mathematician)|Edward Wright]] on the [[George Clifford, 3rd Earl of Cumberland|Earl of Cumberland]]'s raiding [[Azores Voyage of 1589|expedition to the Azores]] to capture Spanish [[galleon]]s.<ref name=ODNB/>

Beginning in August 1591, Hues joined Cavendish on another attempt to circumnavigate the globe. Sailing on the ''Leicester'', they were accompanied by the explorer [[John Davis (English explorer)|John Davis]] on the ''Desire''. Cavendish and Davis agreed that they would part company once they had cleared the [[Strait of Magellan]] between [[Chile]] and [[Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego]], as Davis intended to sail to America to search for the [[Northwest Passage]]. The expedition was ultimately unsuccessful, although Davis did discover the [[Falkland Islands]].<ref>{{citation|author=Margaret Montgomery Larnder|contribution=Davis (Davys), John|contribution-url=http://www.biographi.ca/009004-119.01-e.php?BioId=34283|archive-url=https://archive.today/20240524095856/https://www.webcitation.org/5hNpvaj0i?url=http://www.biographi.ca/009004-119.01-e.php%3FBioId=34283|url-status=dead|archive-date=24 May 2024|title=Dictionary of Canadian Biography Online|year=2000|access-date=9 June 2009|title-link=Dictionary of Canadian Biography}}</ref> In the meantime, delayed in small harbours in the Strait with crew members dying from the cold, illness and starvation, Cavendish turned back eastwards to return to England. He was plagued by [[mutiny|mutinous]] crewmen, and also by natives and Portuguese who attacked his sailors seeking food and water on shore. Increasingly depressed, Cavendish died in 1592 somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean, possibly a suicide.<ref name="Markham xxxv"/><ref>{{citation|author=David Judkins|contribution=Cavendish, Thomas (1560–1592)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=on2ShbwVzp4C&pg=PA203|editor=Jennifer Speake|editor-link=Jennifer Speake|title=Literature of Travel and Exploration: An Encyclopedia|volume=1|location=New York, N.Y.|publisher=Fitzroy Dearborn|year=2003|pages=202–204 at 203|isbn=978-1-57958-425-2}}</ref>

During the voyage, Hues made [[astronomy|astronomical]] observations of the [[Crux|Southern Cross]] and other stars of the [[Southern Hemisphere]] while in the South Atlantic, and also observed the variation of the compass there and at the [[Equator]]. He returned to England after Cavendish died,<ref name="Markham xxxvi">Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xxxvi.</ref> and published his discoveries in the work ''Tractatus de globis et eorum usu'' (''Treatise on Globes and Their Use'', 1594),<ref>{{citation|author=Robert Hues|title=Tractatus de globis et eorum usu: accommodatus iis qui Londini editi sunt anno 1593, sumptibus Gulielmi Sandersoni civis Londinensis, conscriptus à Roberto Hues [Treatise on Globes and their Use: Adapted to those which have been Published in London in the Year 1593, at the Expense of William Sanderson, a London Resident, Written by Robert Hues]|location=London|publisher=In ædibus Thomæ Dawson [in the house of Thomas Dawson]|year=1594|oclc=55576175}} (in [[Latin]]).</ref> which he dedicated to Raleigh.<ref name=ODNB/> The book was written to explain the use of the terrestrial and celestial globes that had been made and published by [[Emery Molyneux]] in late 1592 or early 1593.<ref>{{citation|author=Helen M. Wallis|author-link=Helen Wallis|title=The first English globe: A recent discovery|journal=[[The Geographical Journal]]|volume=117|issue=3|year=1951|page=280|doi=10.2307/1791852|jstor=1791852|bibcode=1951GeogJ.117..275W }}</ref> Apparently, the book was also intended to encourage English sailors to use practical astronomical navigation,<ref name=ODNB/> although [[Lesley Cormack]] has observed that the fact it was written in [[Latin]] suggests that it was aimed at scholarly readers on the Continent.<ref name=Cormack>{{citation|author=Lesley B. Cormack|author-link= Lesley Cormack |title=The Commerce of Utility: Teaching Mathematical Geography in Early Modern England|journal=Science & Education|date=March 2006|volume=15|issue=2–4|pages=305–322 at 311|doi=10.1007/s11191-004-7690-2|bibcode = 2006Sc&Ed..15..305C |s2cid= 145588853 }}</ref> In 1595, William Sanderson, a London merchant who had largely financed the globes' construction, presented a small globe together with Hues's "Latin booke that teacheth the use of my great globes"<ref>{{citation|author=R. A. Skelton|author-link=Raleigh Ashlin Skelton|author2=John Summerson|author-link2=John Summerson|title=A Description of Maps and Architectural Drawings in the Collection made by William Cecil, First Baron Burghley, Now at Hatfield House|location=Oxford|publisher=Printed for presentation to the members of the [[Roxburghe Club]]|year=1971|oclc=181678336}}; {{cite ODNB|author=Susan M. Maxwell|contribution=Molyneux, Emery (''d.'' 1598)|title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography|edition=Online|location=Oxford|date=September 2004|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/50911|last2=Harrison|first2=B.|title-link=Dictionary of National Biography}}</ref> to [[Robert Cecil, 1st Earl of Salisbury|Robert Cecil]], a [[politician|statesman]] who was [[spymaster]] and minister to [[Elizabeth I of England|Elizabeth&nbsp;I]] and [[James I of England|James&nbsp;I]]. Hues's work subsequently went into at least 12 other printings in Dutch (1597, 1613 and 1622), English (1638 and 1659), French (1618) and Latin (1611, 1613, 1617, 1627, 1659 and 1663).<ref>Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', pp. xxxviii–xl.</ref> In his book ''An Accidence or The Path-way to Experience: Necessary for all Young Sea-men'' (1626),<ref>{{citation|author=John Smith|author-link=John Smith of Jamestown|title=An Accidence or The Path-way to Experience. Necessary for all Young Sea-men, or those that are Desirous to Goe to Sea, briefly shewing the Phrases, Offices, and Words of Command, belonging to the Building, Ridging, and Sayling, a Man of Warre; and how to Manage a Fight at Sea. Together with the Charge and Duty of every Officer, and their Shares: Also the Names, VVeight, Charge, Shot, and Powder, of all Sorts of Great Ordnance. With the Vse of the Petty Tally. Written by Captaine Iohn Smith sometimes Governour of Virginia, and Admirall of New England|location=London|publisher=Printed &#91;by [[Nicholas Okes]]&#93; for Ionas Man, and Benjamin Fisher, and are to be sold at the signe of the Talbot, in Aldersgate streete|year=1626|oclc=55198107}}. Original in the Henry E. Huntington Library and Art Gallery (now [[The Huntington Library]]) in [[San Marino, California]]. ''Accidence'' is the branch of [[grammar]] that deals with the accidents or [[inflection]]s of words. The term came to mean a book about the [[wikt:rudiment|rudiments]] of grammar, and was extended to the rudiments or first principles of any subject: see {{citation|contribution=accidence<sup>2</sup>|contribution-url=http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/1049?rskey=yLIzcm&result=2&isAdvanced=false#eid|title=OED Online|edition=2nd|location=Oxford|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=1989|access-date=23 July 2016|title-link = Oxford English Dictionary}}</ref> [[John Smith of Jamestown|John Smith]], who founded the first permanent English settlement in North America at [[Jamestown, Virginia]], listed Hues's book among the works that a young seaman should study.<ref>{{citation|author=Susan Rose|title=Mathematics and the Art of Navigation: The Advance of Scientific Seamanship in Elizabethan England|journal=Transactions of the Royal Historical Society|year=2004|volume=6|pages=175–184 at 177|doi=10.1017/S0080440104000192|issue=14|s2cid=178295770}}</ref>

[[File:RobertHues-TractaetGlobe-AertscheGlobe-1623.jpg|thumb|left|upright|A drawing of [[Emery Molyneux|Molyneux]]'s terrestrial globe from ''Tractaet ofte Handelinge van het gebruyck der Hemelscher ende Aertscher Globe'', the 1623 Dutch version of Hues's ''Tractatus de globis'']]

''Tractatus de globis'' begins with a letter by Hues dedicated to Raleigh that recalled geographical discoveries made by Englishmen during Elizabeth I's reign. However, he felt that his countrymen would have surpassed the [[Spain|Spaniards]] and [[Portugal|Portuguese]] if they had a complete knowledge of [[astronomy]] and [[geometry]], which were essential to successful navigation.<ref>Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xli.</ref> In the preface of the book, Hues rehearsed arguments that proved the earth is a sphere, and refuted opposing theories.<ref>Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', pp. xli–xlii.</ref> The treatise was divided into five parts. The first part described elements common to Molyneux's terrestrial and celestial globes, including the circles and lines inscribed on them, zones and climates, and the use of each globe's wooden horizon circle and brass meridian.<ref>Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', pp. xlii–xliii.</ref> The second part described [[planet]]s, [[fixed stars]] and [[constellation]]s; while the third part described the lands and seas shown on the terrestrial globe, and discussed the length of the [[Equator|circumference of the earth]] and of a [[degree (angle)|degree]] of a [[great circle]].<ref name="Markham xlii">Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xlii.</ref> Part 4, which Hues considered the most important part of the work, explained how the globes enabled seamen to determine the sun's position, latitude, course and distance, amplitudes and [[azimuth]]s, and time and [[declination]].<ref>Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', pp. xlii and xlvi.</ref> The final part of the work contained a treatise inspired by Harriot on [[rhumb line]]s.<ref name="Markham xlii"/><ref>{{citation|author=D[avid] B. Quinn|author2=J[ohn] W[illiam] Shirley|title=A Contemporary List of Hariot References|journal=Renaissance Quarterly|year=1969|volume=22|issue=1|pages=9–26 at 13–14|doi=10.2307/2858975|jstor=2858975|s2cid=164132753 }}</ref> In the work, Hues also published for the first time the six fundamental navigational propositions involved in solving what was later termed the "nautical triangle" used for [[plane sailing]]. Difference of latitude and departure (or [[longitude]]) are two sides of the triangle forming a [[right angle]], the distance travelled is the [[hypotenuse]], and the angle between difference of latitude and distance is the course. If any two elements are known, the other two can be determined by plotting or calculation using tables of [[Tangent (trigonometric function)|sines]], [[Tangent (trigonometric function)|tangents]] and [[Secant function|secants]].<ref>{{citation|author=Derek Howse|chapter=Astronomical Navigation [pt. 8.18]|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f5FqsDPVQ2MC&q=%22robert+hues%22&pg=PA1128|editor=[[Ivor Grattan-Guinness|I[vor] Grattan-Guinness]]|title=Companion Encyclopedia of the History and Philosophy of the Mathematical Sciences|location=Baltimore, Md.|publisher=[[Johns Hopkins University Press]]|year=2003|isbn=978-0-8018-7397-3|pages=1128, 1129, 1132}}</ref>

In the 1590s, Hues continued to have dealings with Raleigh – he was one of the executors of Raleigh's will<ref name="Markham xxxvi"/> – and he may have been the "Hewes" who dined with Northumberland regularly in 1591. He later became a servant of [[Thomas Grey, 15th Baron Grey de Wilton|Thomas Grey]], the 15th and last [[Baron Grey de Wilton]] (1575–1614). For participating in the [[Bye Plot]], a conspiracy by Roman Catholic priest [[William Watson (priest)|William Watson]] to kidnap James&nbsp;I and force him to repeal anti-Catholic legislation, Grey was [[attainder|attainted]] and forfeited his title in 1603. The following year, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London. Grey was given consent for Hues to stay in the Tower with him.<ref name=ODNB/> Between 1605 and 1621, Northumberland was also confined in the Tower; he was suspected of involvement in the [[Gunpowder Plot]] of 1605 because his relative [[Thomas Percy (plotter)|Thomas Percy]] was among the conspirators.

In 1616, following Grey's death, Hues began to be "attendant upon th'aforesaid Earle of Northumberland for matters of learning",<ref>{{citation|author=John W[illiam] Shirley|title=Thomas Harriot: A Biography|location=Oxford|publisher=[[Oxford University Press|Clarendon Press]]|year=1983|isbn=978-0-19-822901-8|page=577}}</ref> and was paid a yearly sum of £40 to support his research until Northumberland's death in 1632.<ref name=ODNB/><ref name="Markham xxxvi"/> Wood stated that Harriot, Hues and Warner were Northumberland's "constant companions, and were usually called the Earl of Northumberland's Three Magi. They had a table at the Earl's charge, and the Earl himself did constantly converse with them, and with Sir Walter Raleigh, then in the Tower".<ref>{{citation|author=Anthony à Wood|author-link=Anthony Wood (antiquary)|title=Athenae Oxoniensis. An Exact History of All the Writers and Bishops who have had their Education in the Most Ancient and Famous University of Oxford, from the Fifteenth Year of King Henry the Seventh, Dom. 1500, to the End of the Year 1690. Representing the Birth, Fortune, Preferment, and Death of all those Authors and Prelates, the Great Accidents of their Lives, and the Fate and Character of their Writings. To which are Added, the Fasti or Annals, of the said University, for the Same Time |volume=1|location=London|publisher=Printed for Tho. Bennett|year=1691–1692|page=485|oclc=70434257 }}: see {{citation|author=Arthur Collins|title=The Peerage of England, or, An Historical and Genealogical Account of the Present Nobility: Containing, the Descent, Original Creations, and most Remarkable Actions, of their Respective Ancestors: Also, the Chief Titles of Honour and Preferment they now Enjoy, with their Marriages and Issue, Continu'd Down to this Present Year, 1709, and the Paternal Coats of Arms of each Family, in Blazon. Collected as well from our best Historians, Publick Records, and other Sufficient Authorities, as from the Personal Informations of most of the Nobility. To which is Prefix'd, an Introduction of the Present Royal Family of Great-Britain, Trac'd thro' its Several Branches down to this Time, and Terminating with the Protestant Succession, as Settled by Act of Parliament|location=London|publisher=Printed by G.J. for Abel Roper and Arthur Collins|year=1709}}. See also {{citation|author=Charles Hutton|author-link=Charles Hutton|contribution=Harriot (Thomas)|url=http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/toc/toc.cgi?page=612;dir=hutto_dicti_078_en_1795;step=textonly|title=A Mathematical and Philosophical Dictionary: Containing an Explanation of the Terms, and an Account of the Several Subjects, Comprized under the Heads of Mathematics, Astronomy, and Philosophy both Natural and Experimental: With an Historical Account of the Rise, Progress, and Present State of these Sciences: Also Memoirs of the Lives and Writings of the Most Eminent Authors, both Ancient and Modern, who by their Discoveries or Improvements have Contributed to the Advancement of them. In Two Volumes, with Many Cuts and Copper-plates|location=London|publisher=Printed by J. Davis, for J. Johnson, in St. Paul's Church-yard; and G.G. and J. Robinson, in Paternoster-Row (reproduced on the website of the Archimedes Project, [[Max Planck Institute for the History of Science]])|year=1795–1796|page=584|oclc=8166998|access-date=10 November 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716104142/http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/toc/toc.cgi?page=612;dir=hutto_dicti_078_en_1795;step=textonly|archive-date=16 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> Together with the scientist Nathanael Toporley and the mathematician Thomas Allen, the men kept abreast of developments in astronomy, mathematics, [[physiology]] and the [[outline of physical science|physical sciences]], and made important contributions in these areas.<ref name=Kargon>Kargon, "The Wizard Earl and the New Science" in ''Atomism in England'', pp. 5–17 at 16.</ref> According to the letter writer [[John Chamberlain (letter writer)|John Chamberlain]], Northumberland refused a pardon offered to him in 1617, preferring to remain with Harriot, Hues and Warner.<ref>{{citation|author=John Chamberlain|author-link=John Chamberlain (letter writer)|editor=Norman Egbert McClure|title=The Letters [Memoirs of the American Philosophical Society, vol. 12, pts. 1–2]|location=Philadelphia, Penn.|publisher=[[American Philosophical Society]]|year=1939|volume=1|page=566|oclc=221477966}}: see Kargon, "The Wizard Earl and the New Science" in ''Atomism in England'', pp. 5–17 at 16.</ref> However, the fact that these companions of Northumberland were his "Three Magi" studying with him in the Tower of London has been regarded as a romanticisation by the antiquarian [[John Aubrey]] and disputed for lack of evidence.<ref name=ODNB/><ref>{{citation|author=John Aubrey|author-link=John Aubrey|editor=Oliver Lawson Dick|title=Aubrey's Brief Lives|location=London|publisher=[[Secker and Warburg]]|year=1975|page=123|oclc=1981442|title-link=Brief Lives}}, critiqued by Shirley, ''Thomas Harriot'', pp. 364–365. See {{citation|author=Allan Chapman|author-link=Allan Chapman (historian)|title=The Astronomical Work of Thomas Harriot (1560–1621)|bibcode=1995QJRAS..36...97C|journal=Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society|year=1995|volume=36|pages=97–107 at 99}}</ref> Hues was tutor to Northumberland's sons: first [[Algernon Percy, 10th Earl of Northumberland|Algernon Percy]], who subsequently became the 10th [[Earl of Northumberland]], at Oxford where he [[matriculation|matriculated]] at [[Christ Church, Oxford|Christ Church]] in 1617; and later Algernon's younger brother Henry in 1622–1623. Hues lived at Christ Church at this time, but may have occasionally attended upon Northumberland at [[Petworth House]] in [[Petworth]], West Sussex, and at [[Syon House]] in London after the latter's release from the Tower in 1622.<ref name=Kargon/> Hues sometimes met Walter Warner in London, and they are known to have discussed the reflection of bodies.<ref name=ODNB/>

==Later life==
[[File:Cathedral oxford.jpg|thumb|[[Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford]], the burial place of Robert Hues]]

In later years, Hues lived in [[Oxford]] where he discussed mathematics and allied subjects with like-minded friends.<ref name=ODNB/><ref>Feingold says that Hues became "a type of private tutor to Oxford men": {{citation|author=Mordechai Feingold|title=The Mathematicians' Apprenticeship: Science, Universities and Society in England, 1560–1640|location=Cambridge|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=1984|page=[https://archive.org/details/mathematiciansap0000fein/page/84 84]|isbn=978-0-521-25133-4|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematiciansap0000fein/page/84}}</ref> Cormack states he was a fellow at the university.<ref name=Cormack/> Under the terms of the will of Thomas Harriot, who died on 2 July 1621, Hues and Warner were given the responsibility of helping Harriot's executor [[Nathaniel Torporley]] to prepare Harriot's mathematical papers for publication. Hues was also required to help price Harriot's books and other possessions for sale to the [[Bodleian Library]].<ref name=ODNB/>

Hues, who did not marry, died on 24 May 1632 in Stone House, [[St Aldate's, Oxford|St. Aldate's]] (opposite the Blue Boar in central Oxford).<ref>In ''Historia et antiquitates universitatis Oxoniensis'' (''History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford'', 1674), vol. 2, p. 361, notice of Hues's death was given under St. Mary Hall as follows: "Oxonii in parochiâ Sancti Aldati, inque Domicilio speciatim lapides [''sic'': lapideo?], e regione insignis Afri [''sic'': Apri?] cærulei, fatis concessit, et in ecclesiâ Ædis Christi Cathedrali humatus fuit an: dom: CIƆDXXXII [''sic'': CIƆDCXXXII]" (He yielded to the [[Parcae|Fates]] at Oxford, in the [[St Aldate's, Oxford|parish of St. Aldate]], specifically in the Stone House, in the neighbourhood of the Blue Boar sign, and was buried in the church of Christ Church Cathedral in the year of our Lord 1532 [''sic'': 1632]). {{citation|title=Historia et antiquitates universitatis Oxoniensis duobus voluminibus comprehensæ [History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford Taken together in Two Volumes]|location=Oxford|publisher=E Theatro Sheldoniano [ [[Sheldonian Theatre]], [[University of Oxford]] ]|year=1674|oclc=13439733}}, was a Latin translation by Richard Peers and Richard Reeve under the direction of Dr. [[John Fell (clergyman)|John Fell]] of an English manuscript by Anthony à Wood which the University purchased in 1670. The manuscript itself was later published as {{citation|author=Anthony à Wood|author-link=Anthony Wood (antiquary)|author2=John Gutch|author-link2=John Gutch (clergyman)|title=The History & Antiquities of the Colleges and Halls in the University of Oxford&nbsp;... Now First Published in English, from the Original Manuscript in the Bodleian Library&nbsp;... with a Continuation to the Present Time, by the Editor, John Gutch. (Appendix to the History and Antiquities of the Colleges and Halls in the University of Oxford&nbsp;... containing Fasti Oxonienses, or a Commentary on the Supreme Magistrates of the University: by Anthony à Wood, M.A. Now First Published in English&nbsp;... with a Continuation to the Present Time, also Additions and Corrections&nbsp;... and Indexes to the Whole, by the Editor, John Gutch.)|location=Oxford|publisher=[[Oxford University Press|Clarendon Press]]|year=1786–1790|oclc=84810015}}. See Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xxxvii, n. 1.</ref> This was the house of John Smith, [[Master of Arts (Oxford, Cambridge and Dublin)|M.A.]], the son of a cook at Christ Church named J. Smith.<ref name="Markham xxxvi"/> In his will, Hues made many small [[bequest]]s to his friends, including a sum of £20 to his "kinswoman" Mary Holly (of whom nothing is known), and 20 [[noble (English coin)|nobles]] to each of her three sisters. He was buried in [[Christ Church Cathedral, Oxford|Christ Church Cathedral]], and a [[monumental brass]] to him was placed in Christ Church with the following inscription:<ref name=ODNB/>

{{blockquote|''Depositum viri literatissimi, morum ac religionis integerrimi, Roberti Husia, ob eruditionem omnigenem ''[sic:'' omnigenam''?]'', Theologicam tum Historicam, tum Scholasticam, Philologicam, Philosophiam, præsertim vero Mathematicam (cujus insigne monumentum in typis reliquit) Primum Thomæ Candishio conjunctissimi, cujus in consortio, explorabundis ''[sic:'' explorabundus''?]'' velis ambivit orbem: deinde Domino Baroni Gray; cui solator accessit in arca Londinensi. Quo defuncto, ad studia henrici Comitis Northumbriensis ibidem vocatus est, cujus filio instruendo cum aliquot annorum operam in hac Ecclesia dedisset et Academiae confinium locum valetudinariae senectuti commodum censuisset; in ædibus Johannis Smith, corpore exhaustus, sed animo vividus, expiravit die Maii 24, anno reparatae salutis 1632, aetatis suæ 79.''<ref>''Historia et antiquitates universitatis Oxoniensis'', vol. 2, p. 534. The brass is also referred to at p. 288: "In laminâ œneâ, eidem pariati [''sic'': parieti?] impactâ talem cernis inscriptionem" (On the copper plate, driven to the same wall, one sees such an inscription). See Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', p. xxxvii, n. 1.</ref>

[Here lies a highly lettered man, of the highest moral and religious integrity, Robert Hues, on account of his erudition in all subjects, both Theology and History, and Rhetoric, Philology, and Philosophy, but especially Mathematics (of which a notable volume [''i.e.'', his book] remains in print). He was most closely associated with Thomas Cavendish, in whose company he explored the world by sail; then with Lord Baron Gray, for whom he came as consoler in the Tower of London. When Gray died, he was summoned to study in the same place with Henry Earl of Northumberland, to teach his son, and when he had worked for some years in this Church [''i.e.'', Christ Church Cathedral], and had decided that the place next to the School [''i.e.'', Christ Church, Oxford] was suitable for his health in his old age, he breathed his last at the house of John Smith, his body exhausted, but with a lively spirit, on 24 May, in the year of our salvation 1632, at the age of 79.]<!--This is a rough translation by [[User:Jacklee]] with much assistance from [[User:Kladderadatsch]]. It was last updated on 20 January 2011 with help from editors at "[[Wikipedia:Reference desk/Archives/Language/2011 January 15#Latin to English translation at "Robert Hues"]]". Knowledgeable editors are invited to improve the translation.-->}}

Hondium [Treatise or Essays on the Use of the Celestial and Terrestrial Globes. Tailored for the Globes which were First Made in England by J. According to Markham, "Introduction", ''Tractatus de globis'', pp. xxxvii–xxxviii, the title of this version is ''Tractaut of te handebingen van het gebruych der hemel siker ende aertscher globe'', and it was printed in Antwerp.</ref>
